sub: Polymorphism, function and operator overloading
q: Function overloading and operator overloading are usually classified as which kind of polymorphism, and on what grounds?

opts.A: Run-time polymorphism, because the correct function is located through the object's vtable
opts.B: Compile-time polymorphism, because the overload is selected from the static types of the arguments while the program is being translated
opts.C: Run-time polymorphism, because the arguments are not known until the program executes
opts.D: Neither, since polymorphism refers only to inheritance hierarchies

exp: Overload resolution is performed entirely by the compiler using the declared types of the argument expressions, and the call that reaches the linker names one specific function, which is why it is also called static or early binding. Run-time polymorphism is the separate mechanism in which a call through a base pointer or reference is dispatched on the dynamic type of the object, and it needs a virtual function to exist at all — options A and C attach that machinery to overloading, which does not use it. Option D is too narrow: dispatching on a hierarchy is one form of polymorphism, not the definition of it.

sub: Polymorphism, function and operator overloading
q: Why is a copy-assignment operator conventionally declared as Vec& operator=(const Vec& other) rather than as void operator=(const Vec& other)?

opts.A: Because a void operator= will not compile
opts.B: Because returning a reference is what tells the compiler to perform a member-by-member copy
opts.C: Because the returned reference is what the destructor uses to release the previous contents
opts.D: Because assignment in C++ is an expression that yields its left operand, so returning Vec& lets a = b = c chain and lets the result be used where a Vec is expected

exp: For the built-in types a = b = c parses as a = (b = c) and the inner assignment yields the assigned-to object, so a user-defined operator= that returns Vec& keeps class types consistent with that behaviour and permits the same chaining. Option A overstates the case, which is what makes it the plausible one: void operator= compiles perfectly well and works for a plain a = b, so the reason for the convention is expressiveness and consistency rather than legality. Returning a reference has no bearing on how members are copied or on destruction.

sub: Polymorphism, function and operator overloading
q: Which of these is a genuine limitation of operator overloading in C++?

opts.A: The precedence, associativity and number of operands of an operator are fixed by the grammar and cannot be altered by an overload, and no new operator token such as ** can be introduced
opts.B: An overloaded operator may not be declared as a non-member function
opts.C: An overloaded operator cannot be given a meaning unrelated to the operator's built-in meaning; the compiler rejects such definitions
opts.D: At most one operator may be overloaded per class

exp: Overloading supplies a new function body for an existing operator token; the parser has already fixed how that token binds, so a * b keeps its precedence relative to a + b whatever the operands are, and a token the grammar does not define cannot be given one. Option C describes a real convention rather than a rule — nothing stops a class from defining operator+ to do something surprising, and the compiler will not complain, which is precisely why the guidance to preserve conventional meaning has to be a matter of discipline. Option B has it backwards, since operators such as << and the symmetric arithmetic ones are normally non-members.

sub: Polymorphism, function and operator overloading
q: A class Point needs to support cout << p. Why must the stream insertion operator be overloaded as a non-member function, typically declared a friend of Point?

opts.A: Because operator<< is a bitwise operator and member overloads of bitwise operators are not permitted
opts.B: Because friend functions execute faster, avoiding the this pointer
opts.C: Because a member operator<< would belong to Point, making the call p << cout instead; the left operand of cout << p is the ostream, which is a standard library class the programmer cannot add members to
opts.D: Because std::ostream is abstract and cannot appear as a parameter of a member function

exp: The left operand of a binary member operator is the object the function is called on, so Point::operator<< would only serve expressions of the form p << something; making the ostream the left operand would mean adding a member to std::ostream, which is not open to modification. A non-member taking (std::ostream&, const Point&) puts both operands in the parameter list and is declared a friend only when it needs access to private members — the non-member part is required, the friend part is a convenience. Option D is simply untrue of std::ostream, and nothing about the bitwise origin of the token restricts where it may be overloaded.

sub: Polymorphism, function and operator overloading
q: A Buffer class declares both int& operator[](int i) and const int& operator[](int i) const. Given Buffer b; and const Buffer& cb = b;, which overload does each of b[0] and cb[0] select?

opts.A: Both select the const version, because the const overload is declared second
opts.B: b[0] selects the non-const version and cb[0] selects the const version, because the constness of the object the operator is called on participates in overload resolution
opts.C: Both select the non-const version, since b and cb name the same object
opts.D: The pair is ill-formed, because two operators with identical parameter lists cannot be overloaded

exp: The cv-qualification of the implicit object parameter is part of the member function's signature, so the two declarations are genuinely distinct overloads and resolution matches the non-const one to a non-const object and the const one to a const object or reference. This is the standard way to let b[0] = 7 work while still permitting reads through a const reference, and it is why option D is wrong — the parameter lists match but the implicit object parameters do not. Option C mistakes identity of the object for the static type used to reach it: resolution happens at compile time and sees only that cb is a reference to const.

sub: Inheritance, virtual functions and pointers to objects
q: A C++ class is declared as class D : private B. Which statement about the resulting access is correct?

opts.A: B's public members become protected in D, and B's protected members become private in D
opts.B: B's private members become reachable inside D's member functions, because the inheritance itself is private
opts.C: B's public and protected members become private members of D: D's own member functions can still use them, but a class further derived from D cannot
opts.D: Code outside D may still convert a D* to a B* implicitly, because the B subobject exists whatever the inheritance specifier says

exp: Private inheritance lowers every accessible base member to private in the derived class, which stops the chain one level down: D can use them, anything derived from D cannot. Option D is the tempting one because the B subobject genuinely is there, but the derived-to-base pointer conversion is itself an access-controlled operation and is available only inside D's members and friends.

sub: Inheritance, virtual functions and pointers to objects

opts.A: It compiles and writes both inherited copies of id, since they share a name and a type
opts.B: It is rejected as an ambiguous reference, because ReadWriter contains two Storage subobjects; declaring Reader and Writer as struct Reader : virtual Storage and struct Writer : virtual Storage gives ReadWriter a single shared Storage subobject
opts.C: It compiles and writes the copy inherited through Writer, because Writer is listed last in ReadWriter's base list
opts.D: It compiles, but which of the two copies is written is unspecified, so the result varies between compilers

exp: This is the diamond: ReadWriter inherits Storage twice, so the unqualified name id names two distinct members and the lookup is ambiguous at compile time, not at run time. Virtual inheritance on the two intermediate classes is the language's answer, collapsing them to one shared base subobject; nothing about base-list ordering makes the compiler pick one, which is why the last-listed-wins option is wrong.

sub: Inheritance, virtual functions and pointers to objects

opts.A: B1
opts.B: B2
opts.C: D2
opts.D: D1

exp: Which function body runs is decided at run time from the object's dynamic type, so D::f executes, but a default argument is not part of the dispatch: the compiler substitutes it at the call site from the static type of the expression, which is B*, giving n = 1. D2 is the trap for assuming the default travels with the overriding function; this mismatch is exactly why overriding a virtual function with a different default argument is considered a defect in a design.

sub: Inheritance, virtual functions and pointers to objects

opts.A: B
opts.B: D
opts.C: BD
opts.D: Nothing is guaranteed; the behaviour is undefined and either letter may appear

exp: While a base constructor is running, the object is not yet a D: its dynamic type is B, so a virtual call from inside B's constructor resolves to B::speak. The behaviour is fully defined here, which rules out the undefined-behaviour option. It would become undefined if speak() were declared pure virtual, and that holds whether or not the pure virtual function is given a definition — [class.abstract] makes a virtual call to a pure virtual function from a constructor or destructor of an abstract class undefined either way, so providing a body does not rescue it.

sub: Inheritance, virtual functions and pointers to objects
q: A function is declared void render(Shape s);. Shape has a virtual draw(), and Circle derives publicly from Shape and overrides draw(). A Circle object is passed to render, yet inside render the call s.draw() runs Shape::draw. What explains this, and what fixes it?

opts.A: Circle::draw must carry the virtual keyword of its own; the base's declaration does not extend to the derived class
opts.B: render takes its parameter by value, so only the Shape subobject is copied: the object is sliced and the parameter's dynamic type really is Shape. Declaring the parameter const Shape& restores dynamic dispatch
opts.C: Dynamic dispatch occurs only through a pointer, so the parameter must be changed to Shape*
opts.D: Shape's copy constructor should be declared virtual so that the Circle part of the object is copied as well

exp: A by-value parameter is a fresh Shape object copy-constructed from the Shape subobject of the argument, so the Circle part is discarded and there is no derived object left to dispatch to. Option C is the near-miss: references dispatch dynamically just as pointers do, so a const Shape& parameter is enough, and option D fails because a constructor can never be virtual.

sub: Inheritance, virtual functions and pointers to objects
q: Which statement about a pure virtual function in C++ is correct?

opts.A: It may be given a definition outside the class body, and an override can then invoke it through a qualified call such as Base::f(); the class remains abstract either way
opts.B: The = 0 specifier and a function body are mutually exclusive, so any attempt to define the function is rejected
opts.C: Supplying a definition for it makes the class concrete, so objects of that class can then be created
opts.D: Only a pure virtual destructor may be given a definition; every other pure virtual function must be left undefined

exp: Declaring a function pure virtual says only that a derived class must provide an override, not that the base may not supply shared code, so an out-of-class definition is legal and is reachable through a qualified call that suppresses dispatch. What the definition does not do is change abstractness, which is what option C gets wrong: the class stays abstract because the declaration still carries = 0.

sub: Inheritance, virtual functions and pointers to objects
q: Given class A { }; class B : public A { }; class C : public B { }; which term names this arrangement, and in what order do the three constructor bodies run when a C object is created?

opts.A: Multilevel inheritance; C's constructor body runs first, then B's, then A's
opts.B: Hierarchical inheritance; A's constructor body runs first, then B's, then C's
opts.C: Multilevel inheritance; A's constructor body runs first, then B's, then C's
opts.D: Multiple inheritance; A's constructor runs twice, once for each level of derivation

exp: A chain in which each class derives from the one before it is multilevel inheritance, and construction proceeds from the most-base class outwards, so A's body finishes before B's begins and B's before C's. Hierarchical inheritance is the distractor worth naming: that is several classes deriving from one common base, which is a different shape even though its construction order for any one branch would look the same.

sub: Inheritance, virtual functions and pointers to objects
q: Base* p = new Derived; compiles, but the next line p->reset(); does not, where reset() is a non-virtual member function declared only in Derived. Why, and what is the minimal correct fix?

opts.A: The name reset is looked up in the pointer's static type Base, which declares no such member, so the call is rejected at compile time regardless of what p actually points to; either declare reset() in Base, or obtain a Derived* for the object and call through that
opts.B: The problem is that reset() is not virtual; adding virtual to Derived::reset() would let the compiler find it through a Base*
opts.C: The compiler cannot prove that p is non-null, so guarding the call with if (p) makes it compile
opts.D: Base's destructor is not virtual, which limits what may be reached through a Base* to the base's data members

exp: Member name lookup is a compile-time operation performed on the static type of the expression, and the dynamic type is irrelevant to it, so a member absent from Base's interface is simply not callable through a Base*. Option B is the natural wrong guess: virtual affects which body runs for a name already present in the base, and cannot introduce a name into Base's interface from the derived side.

sub: Inheritance, virtual functions and pointers to objects
q: Shape declares virtual double area() const = 0;. Square defines double area() { return s * s; } and nothing else. The compiler rejects the declaration Square sq; saying that Square is an abstract type. What is wrong?

opts.A: A pure virtual function cannot be overridden by a directly derived class; an intermediate class must sit between Shape and Square
opts.B: Shape must supply a definition for area() before any derived class is permitted to override it
opts.C: Square::area() is not const-qualified, so it does not match Shape::area() const and declares a new function that merely hides the base one; Shape::area remains pure and unoverridden, leaving Square abstract. Writing override on Square::area() would have made the compiler report the mismatch at the declaration
opts.D: Square::area() must itself be marked virtual before it can override the base's pure virtual function

exp: Const-qualification is part of a member function's signature, so area() and area() const are two different functions, and declaring the unqualified one leaves the pure virtual unimplemented while quietly hiding it in Square's scope. Option D is the plausible-sounding one, but virtual is inherited automatically: repeating it changes nothing, and it is precisely because a silent mismatch like this is so easy to write that the override specifier exists.

sub: Inheritance, virtual functions and pointers to objects
q: Consider struct B { virtual B* clone() const; }; struct D : B { D* clone() const override; };. Is D::clone a valid override of B::clone?

opts.A: No; an override must repeat the base's return type exactly, so this declaration is ill-formed
opts.B: No; the differing return type makes D::clone an overload rather than an override, so a call through a B* still selects B::clone
opts.C: Yes, but only because both functions are const-qualified; drop const from both and the return types would have to match exactly
opts.D: Yes; this is a covariant return type, and an override may return D* where the base returns B* provided B is an accessible and unambiguous base class of D. Covariance is permitted for pointers and references only, never for returns by value

exp: C++ relaxes the same-return-type rule for exactly this case, so that a caller holding a D* gets a D* back from clone() without a cast, while a call through B* still returns B* and still dispatches to D::clone. Option B misreads the situation twice over: return type alone can never distinguish overloads, and here the signatures match, so nothing is being overloaded.

sub: Inheritance, virtual functions and pointers to objects
q: A C++ project built with GCC on Linux compiles every translation unit cleanly, but the link fails with 'undefined reference to vtable for Widget'. Widget has several virtual member functions. Which explanation fits?

opts.A: Widget's destructor is not declared virtual, so no vtable is generated for the class at all
opts.B: Widget's key function — the first non-inline, non-pure virtual member function it declares — is declared but never defined; under the Itanium C++ ABI that GCC follows, the vtable is emitted only in the translation unit that defines the key function, so it is never emitted anywhere
opts.C: Two translation units each emitted a copy of Widget's vtable and the linker rejected the conflicting definitions
opts.D: Widget's constructor is not declared virtual, so the vtable pointer is never initialised in the constructed object

exp: The key-function rule exists so that a polymorphic class does not emit its vtable into every translation unit that merely sees the header, and its cost is this diagnostic: forget to define that one function and the vtable has no home, which the linker reports as a missing vtable rather than a missing function. Option C describes the opposite failure and is wrong on both counts — a duplicate would be a multiple-definition error, and vtables are emitted as mergeable symbols anyway; option D is impossible, since a constructor cannot be virtual.

sub: I/O streams and file handling in OOP

opts.A: 3 times, once for each number in the file
opts.B: 4 times, because the newline after 30 leaves eofbit clear until one more extraction is attempted
opts.C: 5 times, because both the space before 30 and the trailing newline are extracted as separate items
opts.D: The body never stops executing, because a failed extraction sets failbit and leaves eofbit clear

exp: Extraction of 30 stops at the newline without touching end-of-file, so eof() is still false and the loop is entered a fourth time; that fourth >> skips the newline, hits end-of-file and fails, and only then is eofbit set. This is why eof() is the wrong loop condition: option D inverts the fact, since a read that fails at end-of-file sets eofbit and failbit together, which is what finally stops the loop.

sub: I/O streams and file handling in OOP
q: An ifstream f has just had an extraction fail at end of file. The program wants to re-read the file from the start, so it calls f.seekg(0, ios::beg) and then extracts again, but nothing is read and the get pointer never moves. What explains this?

opts.A: eofbit permanently marks the stream as exhausted, so no further get operation on that object can succeed
opts.B: The get pointer did move, but the stream's buffer must be re-synchronised with sync() before the repositioned data becomes visible
opts.C: failbit is still set, so the seek and every later operation on the stream are ignored until clear() resets the state flags
opts.D: ios::beg applies only to the put pointer; a get pointer must be rewound with the single-argument form seekg(0)

exp: A stream in a failed state ignores subsequent input operations, and seekg is one of them, so the reposition itself silently does nothing until clear() puts the stream back in a good state. Option A is the tempting one because eofbit was indeed set, but eofbit is not permanent either; clear() resets the whole state word, after which the seek and the reads work normally.

sub: I/O streams and file handling in OOP
q: A program opens an existing record file with fstream f("rec.dat", ios::out | ios::binary), seeks to one record and rewrites it in place. Afterwards the file holds only that single record and every other record is gone. What explains the loss?

opts.A: ios::out on its own truncates the file to zero length at the moment it is opened, so updating an existing file in place needs ios::in | ios::out
opts.B: ios::binary implies ios::trunc, so it was the binary flag that discarded the earlier records
opts.C: The put pointer starts at offset zero, so the write landed on the first record and the stream then shortened the file to the number of bytes written
opts.D: Without ios::app an fstream replaces the whole file on each write rather than at open time

exp: Opening with out and neither in nor app creates-or-truncates the file, exactly like the "w" mode of C stdio, so the records were destroyed before the seek ever ran; combining in with out opens the existing file without truncating and allows read-modify-write in place. Option C is plausible only if you assume truncation happens at write time, whereas the file was already empty when the stream was opened.

sub: I/O streams and file handling in OOP
q: Employee is a struct of fixed-size members with no pointers and no virtual functions, and emp is a non-const Employee object. Which statement writes the raw bytes of emp to an already-open binary ofstream f?

opts.A: f.write(&emp, sizeof(emp));
opts.B: f << emp << sizeof(emp);
opts.C: f.put(reinterpret_cast<char*>(&emp), sizeof(emp));
opts.D: f.write(reinterpret_cast<char*>(&emp), sizeof(emp));

exp: write takes a pointer to characters and a byte count, so the object's address has to be reinterpreted as a char pointer before it can be passed. Option A is the near miss: it is the same call without the cast, and there is no implicit conversion from Employee* to char*, so it does not compile; put transfers one character and takes no length argument.

sub: I/O streams and file handling in OOP

opts.B: 0, because the read failed and no complete request was satisfied
opts.D: 39, because one position is reserved for a terminating null character

exp: read stops when the file is exhausted, transfers the 40 bytes that were available and sets eofbit and failbit; gcount() reports the number of characters the last unformatted input operation actually extracted, which is 40. Option B is the trap: a failed read still transfers what it could, and gcount() is precisely the way to find out how much, so it does not report zero.

sub: I/O streams and file handling in OOP
q: An existing file is opened as ifstream f("img.bin", ios::binary). Which sequence yields the size of the file in bytes?

opts.A: f.seekg(0, ios::beg); streampos n = f.tellg();
opts.B: f.seekg(0, ios::end); streampos n = f.tellg();
opts.C: f.seekp(0, ios::end); streampos n = f.tellp();
opts.D: streamsize n = f.gcount();

exp: Seeking zero bytes relative to ios::end leaves the get pointer just past the last byte, and tellg then reports that offset, which in binary mode is the file's length in bytes. Option C looks symmetrical but an ifstream has only a get pointer, so seekp and tellp are not members of it and the code does not compile; option A reports the offset of the beginning, which is always 0.

sub: I/O streams and file handling in OOP
q: A function creates a local ofstream object, writes several lines through it, and returns without ever calling close(). What happens to data still sitting in the stream's buffer?

opts.A: The file is closed when the object goes out of scope, but whatever is still buffered is dropped, so an explicit flush() is needed before returning
opts.B: The buffer is written out only at normal program termination, when the standard streams are flushed
opts.C: The behaviour is undefined, because an ofstream whose lifetime ends while it is still open leaves the file in an indeterminate state
opts.D: The ofstream destructor runs at the end of the scope and closes the file, and closing flushes the buffer first

exp: A file stream owns its file as a resource: the destructor closes it, and closing flushes any buffered characters to the file, which is why explicit close() calls are optional rather than mandatory. Option A is the common fear and is wrong on the important half; the close performed by the destructor is a real close, not an abandonment of the buffer.

sub: I/O streams and file handling in OOP
q: Why can one fstream object be used both for extraction with >> and for insertion with <<?

opts.A: fstream derives from iostream, which itself derives from both istream and ostream, so it inherits both sets of operations
opts.B: fstream declares its own member overloads of >> and <<, which dispatch on the open mode passed to its constructor
opts.C: fstream holds an ifstream and an ofstream as data members and forwards each operator to the appropriate one
opts.D: Both operators are non-member functions taking an ios& parameter, so they accept any class derived from ios

exp: The stream hierarchy gives fstream its dual capability by inheritance: iostream multiply inherits from istream and ostream, and fstream extends iostream with file-specific members such as open and close. Option D is the closest miss, but the insertion and extraction operations live in ostream and istream, not in ios, so a base of type ios would supply neither.

sub: I/O streams and file handling in OOP
q:
Assume the usual includes, including <iomanip>, and using namespace std. What does this line print?

cout << setfill('*') << setw(5) << 42 << 7 << endl;
exp: setw sets the field width for the next insertion only, after which the width reverts to zero, whereas setfill changes a stream member that persists until it is changed again; so 42 is padded to five characters with asterisks and 7 is printed with no padding at all. Option A is what you would get if width persisted the way fill does, which is exactly the asymmetry being tested.

sub: Exception handling and strings

opts.A: abcX
opts.B: cX
opts.C: acX
opts.D: Xac

exp: Stack unwinding destroys every automatic object that was fully constructed since the try block was entered, in reverse order of construction, and it completes before the handler body runs — so a is destroyed, then c, then X is printed. abcX is the trap: b is never constructed because the throw precedes its declaration, and an object that was never constructed is never destroyed; Xac inverts the guaranteed ordering of unwinding and handler entry.

sub: Exception handling and strings
q: A std::out_of_range is thrown and caught by a handler written catch (const std::exception& e). The handler logs the message and then writes throw e; to pass the exception outwards. An enclosing handler for catch (const std::out_of_range&) never fires, though a plain catch (const std::exception&) on the outer try does. What explains this?

opts.A: throw e; copy-initialises a new exception object of the operand's static type, std::exception, so the dynamic type is lost; a bare throw; would have propagated the original std::out_of_range object untouched
opts.B: throw e; is ill-formed inside a handler, so the compiler rewrites it as a call to std::terminate and the outer try is bypassed entirely
opts.C: throw e; preserves the dynamic type correctly, but a rethrown object can only be matched by a handler that takes it by value, so the outer clause had to be written catch (std::out_of_range)
opts.D: throw e; throws a pointer to the handler's own parameter, which is destroyed as the handler exits, so the outer clause is skipped to avoid matching a dangling object

exp: The operand of a throw-expression is copied into a fresh exception object whose type is the operand's static type, so throwing the base-typed handler parameter discards everything below std::exception; a bare throw; instead reactivates the exception object already in flight, dynamic type intact. Option C inverts the actual rule — handlers routinely match rethrown objects by reference, and catching by value is precisely what would slice again.

sub: Exception handling and strings
q: A function is declared noexcept, and at run time an exception it did not anticipate propagates out of its body. What does the C++ standard say happens?

opts.A: The program is ill-formed: a throw that can reach the boundary of a noexcept function is diagnosed at compile time
opts.B: The exception object is replaced by a std::bad_exception, which then propagates to the caller normally
opts.C: noexcept is only an optimisation hint to the compiler, so the exception propagates to the caller unchanged
opts.D: std::terminate is invoked, and the stack is not guaranteed to have been unwound before that call

exp: Violating a noexcept specification is a run-time event, not a diagnosable one, and the reaction is a call to std::terminate; because unwinding before that call is not required, destructors of intervening automatic objects may never run. Substitution by std::bad_exception belonged to the old dynamic exception specifications (throw(...) lists), which were removed from the language and never applied to noexcept.

sub: Exception handling and strings
q: In the standard exception hierarchy of <stdexcept>, which of these types derives from std::logic_error rather than from std::runtime_error?

opts.A: std::range_error
opts.B: std::length_error
opts.C: std::overflow_error
opts.D: std::underflow_error

exp: std::length_error sits on the logic_error branch: it reports an attempt to produce an object beyond its own maximum size, a fault visible from the program's arguments before the operation is attempted. std::range_error is the near-miss — despite the similar name it is a runtime_error, reported for a result that cannot be represented — and std::overflow_error and std::underflow_error are runtime_error descendants too.

sub: Exception handling and strings
q: In C++11 and later, an exception escapes from a destructor that carries no explicit exception specification and whose base and member destructors are all non-throwing. What is the result?

opts.A: It propagates to the enclosing handler exactly as an exception thrown from an ordinary member function would
opts.B: It propagates normally unless another exception is already in flight, in which case std::terminate is called
opts.C: std::terminate is called, because such a destructor has an implicit non-throwing exception specification
opts.D: std::unexpected is invoked, giving the program the chance to substitute a different exception before propagation

exp: Since C++11 a destructor's implicit exception specification is non-throwing whenever its subobjects' destructors are, so letting an exception out of one is a noexcept violation and calls std::terminate whether or not unwinding is under way. Option B is the pre-C++11 rule that many people still carry — back then the escape was legal on its own and only fatal during unwinding of another exception.

sub: Exception handling and strings
q: A function allocates a buffer with new, performs work that may throw, and calls delete at the end. When the work throws, the buffer leaks. Which change makes the function leak-free without adding any catch clause?

opts.A: Make the pointer static, so its storage survives the unwinding of the function
opts.B: Declare the function noexcept, so the exception cannot escape and the delete is reached
opts.C: Rely on the compiler, which emits the matching delete as part of the unwinding code it generates for the function
opts.D: Hold the allocation in a local std::unique_ptr, whose destructor is run automatically while the stack unwinds

exp: Unwinding runs the destructor of every fully-constructed automatic object, so tying the resource's lifetime to a local object — RAII — releases it on both the normal and the exceptional path with no handler at all. Declaring the function noexcept does not reach the delete: it converts the escape into a call to std::terminate, and the standard does not even require the stack to be unwound first.

sub: Exception handling and strings

opts.A: find() returns 0 when the search fails, and 0 >= 0 is true; the result has to be compared against s.size() instead
opts.B: find() returns std::string::npos on failure, and as an unsigned size_type that is the largest representable value, so p >= 0 can never be false; the test must be p != std::string::npos
opts.C: find() returns -1 on failure, and the comparison widens it to a large positive value only on 64-bit builds, so the bug appears on some platforms and not others
opts.D: The single-character overload of find() treats its argument as a set of characters to search for, so it matched one of the '.' characters

exp: std::string::find reports failure with std::string::npos, a size_type constant equal to the largest value that type can hold, so any comparison of the unsigned result against 0 with >= is vacuously true on every platform. Option C describes the C-style convention of returning -1: npos is indeed defined as size_type(-1), but the result variable is unsigned, so nothing is ever negative and the defect is not platform-dependent. Option D confuses find() with find_first_of().

sub: Exception handling and strings

opts.A: Undefined behaviour: c_str() hands back a pointer into the string's own storage, and a modifying member call such as operator+= invalidates it
opts.B: Well defined, printing abc, because c_str() returns a freshly allocated null-terminated copy that stays valid until the string is destroyed
opts.C: Well defined, because small-string optimisation guarantees that a literal as short as "abc" lives inside the string object itself and can never be moved
opts.D: Well defined, printing the whole concatenated text, because c_str() returns a pointer that follows the string's current contents

exp: c_str() exposes the string's internal character sequence rather than a copy, and any non-const member call other than the few exempted accessors may invalidate the pointers, references and iterators into it — so p is dangling the moment the append runs, regardless of whether reallocation actually occurred. Option C is the standard misreading of small-string optimisation: it is a permitted implementation technique, not a guarantee the standard offers, and an append of this length would exceed any such internal buffer anyway.

sub: Exception handling and strings
q: For a std::string object s, which statement about size(), length() and capacity() is accurate?

opts.A: size() and length() are exact synonyms, and capacity() is at least size(), reporting how many characters the current storage can hold before a reallocation is needed
opts.B: length() returns the count of characters, while size() returns that count plus one for the terminating null character
opts.C: capacity() is always equal to size() until reserve() is called explicitly on the object
opts.D: size() counts characters while length() counts bytes, so the two differ for a string holding multi-byte UTF-8 text

exp: length() is specified as returning size(), and capacity() is a separate quantity never smaller than size() that describes the allocated storage rather than the content. Option D is the most tempting because the two names invite it, but std::string is a sequence of char with no encoding awareness at all: both functions return the same byte count, and neither counts the null that c_str() must supply.
